extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in COVID-19 misinformation
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive Wikipedia article summarizing types, sources, mechanisms, harms, and responses to misinformation about COVID-19, with examples and references. It describes common conspiracy themes, actors, platform dynamics, and countermeasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / scope of COVID-19 misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: False or misleading information, including disinformation and conspiracy theories, about the scale of the COVID-19 pandemic and the origin, prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spreads through social media, text messaging, and mass media. The World Health Organization described an 'infodemic' of incorrect information that poses risks to global health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources and actors spreading misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation has been propagated by celebrities, politicians, other prominent public figures, governments, interest groups, and state-backed operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given include Fox News, individual presenters, political leaders, and government media outlets; motives range from political objectives to financial gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common claim types and themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of COVID-19 misinformation include virus-origin conspiracies (lab leak, bioweapon), false prevention/treatment claims (miracle cures, at-home tests), population-control schemes, 5G networks causing COVID-19, and scapegoating particular groups (ethnic, religious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes many claims are reconfigurations or recontextualisations of true information rather than complete fabrication; it lists numerous specific conspiracy variants and examples (e.g., Plandemic, claims about Bill Gates, 5G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms that amplify misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive biases (jumping to conclusions, confirmation bias), uncertainty among experts, and re-sharing dynamics amplify misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints and unreviewed research, echo chambers, and top-down misinformation from influential figures increase reach; the Reuters Institute study found much misinformation consists of reconfigured true information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of preprints and scientific communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of preprint servers (arXiv, bioRxiv, medRxiv, SSRN) without peer review has contributed to spreading misleading or preliminary findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preprints were shared extensively and used by media more than preprints on other topics; lack of peer review increases risk of misinterpretation and misuse in conspiracy narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform and media amplification dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media platforms, television, and radio can amplify misinformation; different outlets and programs vary in how seriously they present COVID-19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Fox News programs with differing coverage produced measurable differences in local infection and death rates; YouTube, Facebook, and other platforms enacted content moderation (e.g., reducing/removing 5G-COVID content). Speed and moderation delays (YouTube averaged 41 days to remove some COVID-related false videos in early 2020) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms resulting from misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Health harms (worse outcomes, vaccine hesitancy), distrust of news and medical authorities, increased divisiveness and political fragmentation, violence and property damage (e.g., arson attacks on 5G masts), and threats against workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies cited link exposure to certain misinformation to higher infection and death rates; real-world incidents include arson, harassment of engineers, and deaths of public figures who discouraged vaccination.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-backed disinformation and foreign influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple countries have been accused of running state-backed disinformation campaigns to generate panic, sow distrust, undermine democratic debate, or promote political models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and allegations include operations tied to China and Russia, use of government-controlled media outlets, and coordinated social media influence; goals often include geopolitical advantage or domestic political aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virus-origin conspiracy theories and scientific consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Major conspiratorial origin claims include deliberate engineering, lab-leak accidental release, gain-of-function research allegations, and alternative national-origin accusations (e.g., Fort Detrick).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article reports that the consensus among virologists favors natural zoonotic spillover, genomic analyses have ruled out genetic manipulation, and authoritative investigations (WHO joint studies) viewed lab-origin scenarios as unlikely though not definitively ruled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Countermeasures and methods to counter disinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaches include fact-checking, critical thinking, digital/media/health literacy, science communication, platform moderation policies, academic research, and watchdog journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists organisations (e.g., Full Fact, FactCheck.org, International Fact-Checking Network), techniques (truth sandwich, content removal/reduction of recommendations), and institutional responses (WHO's 'infodemic' work and national counter-disinformation units).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial scams and exploitative misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial scams offered at-home tests, purported preventives, and 'miracle' cures, exploiting public fear and misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such scams had financial motives; thousands of people have been arrested for spreading or profiting from COVID-19 misinformation in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and policy responses to misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many countries passed laws against 'fake news' and have taken legal action including arrests related to spreading COVID-19 misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents legal responses and notes controversies around enforcement, free speech, and the effectiveness of punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misinformation promoted by governments and politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments and political leaders sometimes disseminate or amplify misinformation to avoid responsibility, scapegoat others, or influence public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Top-down misinformation, though a minority of content samples in some studies, often generated a majority of social media engagement (e.g., claims about policies or actions by public authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: 5G-specific conspiracy claims and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 5G mobile networks cause COVID-19 or its symptoms led to vandalism and arson attacks on telecommunications masts and harassment of workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article details the spread of the 5G-COVID link, celebrity amplification, platform removals, regulator (Ofcom) responses, and the real-world safety/communications impacts from attacks and threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Targeted stigmatization and xenophobic consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Misinformation fueled xenophobia and scapegoating (e.g., anti-Asian activity, blaming Jews, allegations Muslims spread the virus), resulting in harassment and violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported examples include online vilification, flyers, real-world attacks, and survey data about beliefs linking particular groups to the pandemic.
